1072.title: Raga Asa
1072.hook: the raga of hope, and the ballad sung while the sky is still dark
1072.howItsDone: In gurdwaras the kirtan of the Asa di Var is commonly sung in the early morning, with ragis singing Guru Nanak's pauris and the saloks between them, and the congregation sitting and listening as the day begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Gauri: Sukhmani, peace built section by section, and your line was peace in gauri. A new week starts now.

Long before sunrise, the street outside a gurdwara is still dark, a dog barks somewhere, and a few cars pull in with their headlights on. Inside, the lights are already up. Someone uncovers a harmonium. A tabla player taps the drumhead, listening for the pitch. People drift in with their heads covered, sit on the carpet, and the singing begins before the birds do. What they're singing has a name: the Asa di Var, the ballad in Asa.
screen: `STILL DARK OUTSIDE.` → `THE SINGING STARTS FIRST.` → `THE BALLAD IN ASA.`

segments.voice: Raga Asa is the next great section of the Guru Granth Sahib, right after Gauri. In Punjabi, asa is also an everyday word for hope, and Sikh tradition likes to hear that in the raga's name: the raga of hope. Its mood is described as longing that leans forward, a hope that something good is on its way. That fits the hour. By Sikh custom the Asa di Var belongs to the morning, sung in gurdwaras while the day is still breaking. A var is a ballad, built of stanzas called pauris, with short verses called saloks set between them. In this one, the saloks come from Guru Nanak and Guru Angad. Here's one of Guru Angad's, in plain English. If a hundred moons rose, and a thousand suns climbed the sky, with all that light there would still be deep darkness without the Guru. Heard at dawn, that lands differently. The sun is coming up anyway; the salok says outside light isn't the whole story. There's a light the Sikh Gurus point to that a sunrise can't supply, the light of the Guru's word. So the ballad is sung right at the edge of morning, while one kind of light is arriving, to ask for the other. Hope at dawn, then, isn't forced cheer. It's facing the day before it has shown its hand, and starting it with the Word.
screen: `ASA: THE RAGA OF HOPE.` · `SUNG AS THE DAY BREAKS.` · `A HUNDRED MOONS, A THOUSAND SUNS.` · `STILL DARK WITHOUT THE GURU.` · then, large: `HOPE AT DAWN.`

segments.voice: Let your breath slow and picture the sky just before sunrise, not dark, not light, that gray-blue in between. Let one real hope come up, small or large, for today or for someone you love, and let it sit there in the half-light without polishing it. If you pray, say Waheguru once and leave the hope with it; if you don't, keep it company quietly.
Raga Asa. The raga tradition hears as hope, home of the Asa di Var, the ballad sung while the morning breaks. Today's word.
Your line: hope at dawn. One kind of light arrives while the ballad asks for the other. See you tomorrow.

1073.title: A hymn in Asa
1073.hook: the hymn that opens Asa asks where the door is
1073.howItsDone: Sikhs meet So Dar in daily prayer: a version of it is part of the Japji, and it is sung or recited as part of the Rehras in the evening. In kirtan it is also sung as a shabad of Raga Asa.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Asa, the raga of hope and its ballad sung before sunrise, and your line was hope at dawn.

Some songs you meet in more than one room. You hear one at a wedding, then in a car, then hummed by someone at the sink, and each time it sounds a little different. The Guru Granth Sahib has a hymn like that. A Sikh who has prayed the Japji in the morning has said it. A Sikh who has prayed the Rehras in the evening has said it. And open the Granth to the first page of Raga Asa, and there it is again, standing at the door of the whole section.
screen: `ONE SONG, MORE THAN ONE ROOM.` → `MORNING, EVENING, AND ASA.` → `A HYMN AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: It's called So Dar, from its first words, that door. Guru Nanak opens with a question, given here in plain English: what is that door, what is that house, where you sit and take care of everything? A few days ago, with the string instruments, you heard part of the answer from the Japji: instruments and players beyond counting. Here it goes on. The winds sing, the waters sing, fire sings. The keepers of what's right and wrong sing. The truthful, the contented, the brave. And the hymn admits its list will never be finished: many others sing, it says, whom Nanak can't even call to mind. Notice what Guru Nanak doesn't do. He never gives the door an address. No hill, no temple. Then listen to how the hymn ends, the part a first hearing rushes past. That One, it says, is the King, the King over kings, and Nanak lives within that will. The question was where. The answer, in the end, is how: stand inside the will, and you're already at the door. That's why it opens Asa so well. At dawn, the raga's first hymn asks where God lives and answers with a way to live the day. Asa holds more as you go on: the Patti, a hymn built on the letters of a child's writing board, and the dawn ballad itself. But the way into the section is a door, a song, and a will to live inside.
screen: `SO DAR: THAT DOOR.` · `WHAT IS THAT HOUSE?` · `WIND, WATER, FIRE, SINGING.` · `NANAK LIVES WITHIN THAT WILL.` · then, large: `THE DAWN RAGA.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes if that's comfortable and start with the nearest sound, your breath, a fridge humming, traffic, wind, letting each one count as a voice in that crowd at the door. Then reach a little farther for the next sound, and the next, letting each join in without naming it for long. If you pray, say Waheguru under your breath, adding one more voice; if you don't, simply keep listening outward.
A hymn in Asa. So Dar, that door, the hymn that opens Raga Asa, which hears all creation singing where God sits. Today's word.
Your line: the dawn raga. The question was where, and the answer was how: within that will. Go gently.

1074.title: Raga Gujri
1074.hook: a quiet morning raga, devotion that doesn't announce itself
1074.howItsDone: Ragis sing shabads written in Gujri in Raga Gujri, since in Sikh kirtan the raga is set by the heading of the shabad; tradition places Gujri in the morning hours.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Asa: So Dar, where all creation sings at God's door, and your line was the dawn raga.

What does devotion sound like when nobody's watching? Not the big festival, not the packed hall. Something smaller. A grandmother who covers her head and murmurs a line before she lights the stove. A man who wipes down the steps of the gurdwara before anyone arrives and leaves before anyone thanks him. A teenager with one earbud in on the bus, listening to kirtan at low volume. None of it is loud. All of it is meant. The Guru Granth Sahib has a raga with that temperament.
screen: `DEVOTION WITH NO AUDIENCE.` → `SMALL, MEANT, UNSEEN.` → `RAGA GUJRI.`

segments.voice: Gujri comes after Asa in the Granth's order of ragas. Tradition places it in the morning, and its mood is usually described as quiet and devotional: not Asa's forward lean of hope, but something more settled, like someone who has already turned toward God and simply stays turned. Its hymns come from several of the Gurus, and from Bhagats too. Here's a line from Guru Amar Das in Gujri, in plain English: serve the Lord, and serve no other. It's short, and it doesn't raise its voice. That's a fair picture of the raga. Why would quiet devotion need its own music? Because a lot of devotion is quiet. Sikh practice has its great public moments, the processions, the gatherings, the langar lines. But it also lives in small repeated acts: reciting a bani in the morning, a whispered Waheguru, sweeping a floor. Gujri gives that side of faith a sound. It doesn't try to stir a crowd; it keeps company with one person. One more thing. The raga is named in the shabad's own heading, so in the tradition of singing the Granth in its ragas, the text chooses the music, not the singer's mood that day. A shabad headed Gujri is set to be sung in Gujri. So the quiet is part of the instruction: the Guru set these words to be heard softly, and the music guards that.
screen: `AFTER ASA, A SETTLED MOOD.` · `SERVE THE LORD, AND NO OTHER.` · `MUSIC FOR THE QUIET SIDE OF FAITH.` · `THE TEXT CHOOSES THE RAGA.` · then, large: `QUIET DEVOTION.`

segments.voice: Breathe a little more softly than usual, as if someone nearby were asleep, and think of one small thing you do faithfully that nobody notices: a call to a parent, feeding a pet on time, a glass of water for someone else. Let it count, without making it bigger. If you pray, whisper Waheguru once, as quietly as you can and still hear it; if you don't, let the quiet itself be enough.
Raga Gujri. A raga tradition places in the morning, quiet and devotional, music for the faith that doesn't announce itself. Today's word.
Your line: quiet devotion. In Gujri the text chooses the music, and the music guards the quiet. Until tomorrow.

1075.title: A hymn in Gujri
1075.hook: a crane flies far from her chicks; who feeds them?
1075.howItsDone: Guru Arjan's Gujri hymn about the anxious mind and the crane is part of the Rehras, the evening prayer Sikhs recite or sing at sunset; in kirtan it is sung in Raga Gujri.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Gujri, music for devotion with no audience, and your line was quiet devotion.

A crane lifts off from a marsh and flies a long way, leaving her chicks behind in the reeds. Who feeds them while she's gone? Who teaches them anything? That question isn't from a nature program. It's from a hymn of Guru Arjan in Raga Gujri, one that a Sikh praying the evening Rehras says aloud. A small surprise: yesterday's raga belongs to the morning, yet some of its hymns are carried into the evening prayer.
screen: `A CRANE FLIES FAR.` → `WHO FEEDS THE CHICKS?` → `A GUJRI HYMN AT EVENING.`

segments.voice: The hymn opens by talking to the mind, in plain English: why, mind, do you keep scheming and straining, when the Lord himself is already busy with your care? Then the pictures come. In rocks and stones the Creator places living things, and sets their food in front of them. Then the crane. She flies far away, her chicks are left behind, and no one is there to feed them or teach them to peck. Think about it in your mind, the hymn says. Who looks after them? Guru Arjan isn't telling anyone to stop working; Sikh teaching prizes honest labor. The target is the anxious part of the mind that plans every outcome as if everything rested on it, still running the numbers at two in the morning. Against that, the hymn sets a slower trust: you do your part, and the care was there before you started. The same raga holds a very different voice. Bhagat Trilochan, one of the saints whose words the Gurus gathered into the Granth, asks a sharper question in Gujri: at the very end, what fills the mind? Thoughts of wealth, of wife and sons, of a fine mansion, each one shapes what comes next, he says, and only the one who remembers the Lord goes free. Two voices, one raga. One soothes an anxious mind; one wakes a distracted one. Both bring it back to the same place: steady, unshowy devotion, pointed at what matters.
screen: `WHY SCHEME AND STRAIN, MIND?` · `FOOD SET OUT IN THE ROCKS.` · `WHO FEEDS THE CRANE'S CHICKS?` · `TRILOCHAN: WHAT FILLS THE MIND AT THE END?` · then, large: `DEVOTION IN GUJRI.`

segments.voice: Breathe out longer than you breathe in, find the plan your mind keeps rehearsing today, the email, the bill, the conversation, and picture setting it on the floor beside you; it'll still be there after. For now, picture the crane's chicks in the reeds, fed by no effort of their own. If you pray, say Waheguru and let the worry rest there; if you don't, let your hands lie open.
A hymn in Gujri. Guru Arjan's crane, flying far while her chicks are cared for, and Bhagat Trilochan asking what fills the mind at the end. Today's word.
Your line: devotion in gujri. One voice soothes the anxious mind, and one wakes the distracted one. That's today, done.

1076.title: Raga Devgandhari
1076.hook: a short raga where a Guru admits the mind won't listen
1076.howItsDone: Shabads headed Devgandhari, including Guru Tegh Bahadur's, are sung in kirtan in that raga, whose mood musicians describe as gentle and restrained.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Gujri: the crane's chicks cared for, and Trilochan's question about the end. Your line was devotion in gujri.

This mind won't do a thing I tell it. I've taught it and taught it, and it won't turn from its bad thinking. In plain English, that's how a hymn of Guru Tegh Bahadur begins in the Guru Granth Sahib. No thunder, no threat. Just a tired, honest sentence about the mind, the kind someone might say to a friend after a long week of trying and failing to change a habit. It sits in a small section of the Granth, a raga set between bigger ones.
screen: `THIS MIND WON'T LISTEN.` → `AN HONEST, TIRED SENTENCE.` → `RAGA DEVGANDHARI.`

segments.voice: Devgandhari is a short section. Turn the pages and it's over quickly, next to the long sweeps of Gauri and Asa. Its mood is usually described as gentle and restrained: not grand, not stormy, a soft voice in a quiet room. Its hymns come from Gurus, among them Guru Tegh Bahadur, and his are the ones to stay with. Back to that opening. The hymn goes on to describe the mind plainly: drunk on the world, it fills its own belly and forgets the Lord's praise. Like a dog's tail, it says, it won't be straightened. That's blunt. But listen to the tone. A Guru is speaking about the mind the way a tired parent talks about a stubborn child. No threat, no shouting, just a plain admission that the work is slow, and then the work goes on. The last line turns: Nanak says, remember the Name every day, and the task will be done. That's what a gentle raga is for. Restraint isn't weakness; it's what lets a hard truth be heard without anyone flinching. Sung in a fierce raga, the words might sound like a scolding. Sung in Devgandhari, they sound like company. Trying to change and slipping back is an old story. The Granth doesn't pretend it doesn't happen. It meets it softly, and keeps going: gentle toward the stubborn mind, and gentle in the way the truth is told.
screen: `A SHORT SECTION, A SOFT VOICE.` · `THIS MIND WON'T HEED A WORD.` · `LIKE A DOG'S TAIL, IT WON'T STRAIGHTEN.` · `RESTRAINT LETS TRUTH BE HEARD.` · then, large: `GENTLE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one habit you keep meaning to change and keep not changing, and notice the harsh voice that usually comes with it. Now try the hymn's tone instead, tired maybe, honest, but kind, perhaps simply: not yet, and that's where I am; then let it go and rest. If you pray, say Waheguru softly, once, and leave the habit there; if you don't, let the kindness be the whole practice.

1077.title: Listening in Devgandhari
1077.hook: a short hymn sounds bleak the first time; the second time, you hear where it ends
1077.howItsDone: In kirtan, ragis return to a shabad's refrain line between verses, so the listener hears its center again and again; Guru Tegh Bahadur's Devgandhari hymns are sung in that gentle raga.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Devgandhari, where a Guru speaks gently about a mind that won't listen, and your line was gentle.

A text message arrives: we need to talk. Read it once, fast, and it can sound like trouble. Read it again, slowly, and you notice the little smile at the end. Same words, different message. Speed changes what you hear, and short pieces are the easiest to rush, because they're over before you've arrived. Devgandhari is a short section of the Granth, and today's hymn from it is short too. Both reward the opposite of rushing.
screen: `READ ONCE, FAST.` → `READ AGAIN, SLOWLY.` → `SHORT THINGS GET RUSHED.`

segments.voice: Take one of Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns in Devgandhari. Hear it once, quickly, and here's roughly what lands, in plain English: in this world I have seen that love is false. Everyone is attached to their own comfort, whether spouse or friend. Everyone says mine, mine, and binds the heart to self-interest. At the end, no one goes along. It sounds bleak, and a first listen might stop right there and file it under gloomy. Now hear it again, slowly. The hymn speaks to the foolish mind that still doesn't understand, though the Guru keeps teaching it: yesterday's gentleness, the patient voice. And then the last line, the one a rushed ear misses: Nanak says the one who sings the songs of God crosses the fearful ocean. The hymn doesn't end in the dark. It ends on singing, which is exactly what the listener is hearing at that moment. Heard slowly, a short hymn that seemed a single mood has a shape: a hard look at things, a patient word to the mind, and a turn toward the Name. The Guru set it in a gentle raga, so even the hard opening is sung softly, and the singing carries you to the end. So listen twice: the first time, let the words go by; the second time, slowly, listen for where the hymn ends up.

1078.title: Raga Bihagra
1078.hook: a raga for late at night, colored by separation
1078.howItsDone: Shabads headed Bihagra are sung in that raga in kirtan, and tradition places it in the late hours of the night; its chants by Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan are sung as songs of the soul's longing for God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, listening in Devgandhari: a short hymn heard twice, and its turn toward singing. Your line was twice, slowly. Today the week ends, and the day does too.

The house is asleep. The dishes are done, the phone is face down, and the only light is a lamp or a streetlight through the curtain. At this hour some people find themselves talking to their own heart, quietly, the way you'd talk to a child who can't sleep. Daytime is loud enough to drown that voice out; night isn't. The Granth has a raga for this hour, and in it a Guru speaks to his own soul. This week began at dawn. It ends here, at night.
screen: `THE HOUSE IS ASLEEP.` → `TALKING TO ONE'S OWN HEART.` → `FROM DAWN TO NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Bihagra is a night raga. Tradition sets it for the late hours, and its mood is colored by separation, the ache of being apart from the one you love. In the Guru Granth Sahib that ache has a direction: the beloved is God, and the one waiting is the soul. Guru Ram Das has chants in Bihagra that keep calling to the singer's own soul with a tender word, jindurie, something like my dear life, my little soul, urging it again and again toward the Name. It's how a person might talk to themselves late at night, when sleep won't come: come on, dear one, remember what matters. This isn't despair. In these chants, separation is a kind of love. You only miss what you're bound to; the longing is the sign the bond is real, and the hymns turn the ache into a reason to remember. Now look back at the week, because the ragas made a day. Asa met the dawn with hope, opening with a hymn that hears all creation singing at God's door. Gujri, quiet devotion, with a crane flying far while her chicks are cared for. Devgandhari, gentle, a Guru admitting the mind won't listen, and a short hymn heard twice. And now Bihagra, at night, longing. The same Word, through different hours.
screen: `A NIGHT RAGA, COLORED BY SEPARATION.` · `JINDURIE: MY DEAR LIFE.` · `LONGING MEANS THE BOND IS REAL.` · `THE WEEK: DAWN, QUIET, GENTLE, NIGHT.` · then, large: `NIGHT LONGING.`

segments.voice: Dim whatever you can, the screen, the lights, your eyes, and listen to the late sounds that come far apart, a distant car, the house settling, letting the silence between them be part of what you hear. If a longing rises in one of those gaps, let it come, and let it settle back into the quiet without chasing it. If you pray, set one Waheguru into a gap; if you don't, simply rest in the spaces.
Raga Bihagra. A night raga colored by separation, where Guru Ram Das calls to his own soul as my dear life. Today's word.
Your line: night longing. You only miss what you're bound to. A week of ragas, done.
